one_line: Tutorial for making agent-generated product videos in Claude Code: plan first, review in the browser, render shots one by one, then add music. Sponsored in part, and the title oversells it.
summary: AI Labs presents a multi-stage workflow for having a coding agent build a short product demo video. They run GPT-6 Astra as the model inside Claude Code, reached through a local proxy (CLI Proxy API) that uses an existing Codex subscription instead of API billing. The setup is mostly delegated to the agent: install the proxy, have the agent configure it, log in to Codex, then point Claude Code's base URL at the local server with the generated local key. The production flow is gated at each stage. First the agent writes a shot-by-shot plan (timing, camera moves, zooms) and shows it in the browser with a comment section; the human iterates on comments and then explicitly "locks" the plan. Next the agent renders each shot separately at full screen so the camera work can be checked before polish, and only failed shots are regenerated. After that the clips are combined with smoothing and checked by built-in verification tools. The last step is a custom skill that reads the product style from the plan, measures shot-change frequency to pick a tempo, and searches Mixkit for free music. A Luma Ray 3.2 sponsor segment appears in the middle, and the speaker's claim that Astra beats Fable on design rests on one earlier comparison that is not shown.
speakers: AI Labs presenter (not named in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: Route Claude Code to a non-Anthropic model through a local proxy instead of paying per-token API fees.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker calls the API route expensive for video work. They use CLI Proxy API, a local server that exposes an existing Codex subscription to Claude Code. The key it issues is local-only and not a billed API key.

key_ideas.idea: Let the agent do the proxy setup, then run the Codex login yourself.
key_ideas.detail: Install the proxy with brew, then ask the current agent to change its settings and generate a key, mentioning the model you want. The proxy starts automatically. You then run its login command, which opens a browser to sign in to Codex. Finally you set the base URL in Claude Code, paste the key, and choose the model (spoken as 'GPT-6 Astra').

key_ideas.idea: Plan the whole video before rendering anything, and review the plan in the browser.
key_ideas.detail: The prompt gives the app URL, a 30-second length, 16:9 aspect ratio, music but no voiceover, and reference videos (Anthropic and Linear launch videos). The agent renders a per-second plan with camera moves and page actions, plus a comment box. The human iterates and then asks the agent to lock the plan as the final direction.

key_ideas.idea: Render each shot separately at full screen before polishing.
key_ideas.detail: Each shot gets a basic version so camera moves and zooms can be checked. If one shot is wrong, only that shot is redone. In this run some clips were shaky and some zooms did not match the plan, so the speaker asked for fixes before continuing.

key_ideas.idea: Polish and combine only after shot-level approval, and state the timing explicitly.
key_ideas.detail: The polish prompt covers how the camera moves, where it zooms, and when typing should happen, so each shot flows into the next. The agent saves the combined video in the working folder. Some issues (a shot placed too far right) only surfaced in review and had to be named explicitly to fix.

key_ideas.idea: Music should come from a skill that reads the plan and matches shot timing, not from a generic ask.
key_ideas.detail: A plain 'add music' request picks an arbitrary track. The custom skill reads the product style from the plan, measures how often shots change to set beat, searches Mixkit (categories like Calm and Piano), and writes a new version of the video with the track. The skill was created by giving Claude Code the workflow as a prompt and refined over several test rounds. It is shared through the creator's paid community.

key_ideas.idea: The workflow's real value is its review gates: plan lock, per-shot approval, and final verification checks.
key_ideas.detail: Each stage is a checkpoint so that rework is cheap. The speaker says the installed tools already include checks for small visual issues that the final output must pass. The speaker's own argument is that skipping the planning stage wastes hours and tokens.

techniques.name: Route Claude Code to a Codex subscription via a local proxy
techniques.how: 1) Install CLI Proxy API with brew (exact formula not spoken). 2) Ask your current coding agent to configure the proxy and generate a local API key, naming the model you want. 3) Run the proxy's login command and sign in to Codex in the browser. 4) Launch Claude Code with the base URL set to the local proxy address (not Anthropic). 5) Paste the local key and set the model to GPT-6 Astra. The proxy starts automatically afterwards. The key only works on your own machine.
techniques.when: You want a non-Anthropic model in Claude Code for token-heavy work and already pay for the Codex plan. Check the provider's terms first; the video does not discuss this.

techniques.name: Plan-first with browser preview, comments, and an explicit lock
techniques.how: Prompt the agent with: the app URL to inspect, target length and aspect ratio, audio requirements (e.g. music only), and reference videos. Ask it to render the plan in the browser as a per-second timeline with camera moves and page actions, and to include a comment section. Leave comments, ask the agent to revise, and once satisfied ask it to lock the plan as final.
techniques.when: Before any expensive rendering, so that a wrong plan costs one revision cycle instead of hours of generation.

techniques.name: Render shots individually at full resolution, approve, then fix
techniques.how: Ask the agent to open the browser, record each shot at full-screen resolution, and convert each to video. Review the first shot and approve or request changes before generating the rest. Review all clips together, then regenerate only the shots with problems (shake, wrong zoom).
techniques.when: Any multi-shot generated video where camera movement is the thing being checked, and where rework should stay local.

techniques.name: Polish and combine with explicit timing
techniques.how: Prompt the agent to smooth the movement and combine the clips. State the camera path, zoom targets, and when each typing or UI action should happen. After combining, name each problem by time offset (e.g. 'the shot at X is positioned wrong') and ask for a fix. Run the built-in verification checks on the final output.
techniques.when: After shot-level approval, when clips need to join into one continuous video.

techniques.name: Music skill driven by plan style and shot cadence
techniques.how: Give Claude Code a prompt describing the exact workflow: read the product style from the plan, compute shot-change frequency from the timeline to estimate tempo, search Mixkit by category (Calm, Piano), pick a track whose beat fits, and mix it in to produce a new video version. Save it as a skill and invoke it with a slash command.
techniques.when: When generic background-music picks do not fit the cut rhythm. The speaker says the skill was refined over several test rounds.

tools: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI model, accessed through Codex)
Fable (model compared to Astra on design in an earlier video)

numbers.claim: Target video length: 30 seconds, 16:9 layout (9:16 offered as an option for short-form).
Sponsor claim for Luma Ray 3.2 vs Ray 3: about 4x faster and one third the cost, native 1080p. Unverified sponsor marketing.
Speaker says the API-key route is expensive because video creation uses many tokens. No figures given.

hot_takes: The title ('Just Killed AI Video Editing') overstates the content. The workflow is a sequence of human review gates with agent-run rendering, and it depends on a lot of manual iteration.

About a minute is a Luma AI sponsor read, and the most reusable piece (the music skill) is gated behind the creator's paid community. The speaker also points viewers to the Hyperframes tool installation.
Routing a subscription through a local proxy to get a different model is presented as a cost fix with no discussion of whether the provider's terms allow it.
The claim that GPT-6 Astra has better design direction than Fable rests on a single earlier comparison that is not shown here.
The real lesson is the checkpoint discipline (plan lock, shot-level approval, final verification) rather than the specific model choice.

relevance.why: ProsHarness plans, critiques, and runs Claude Code. This video's explicit plan-comment-lock step and per-unit approval before expensive rendering map directly onto that plan stage, but the video is about video generation.
relevance.action: Add an explicit 'locked plan' state after human comment-based revision and before execution in ProsHarness's plan stage, and test whether reviewer comments can drive a revision loop.

relevance.why: The stage gates (plan, per-shot approval, final checks) are a human-in-the-loop pattern for multi-step generation jobs, loosely related to AgentOS's approval flows.
relevance.action: Note the plan-lock then per-unit approval sequence as a reference pattern for long generation jobs; no change needed now.
